questions.q: What is middleware?
questions.explain: Middleware is for work that belongs to every request (headers, CORS, rate limits, timing). It receives context and next; next() runs the next middleware and, at the end, the route.
options: A route that answers every path
A function that runs around the route: it gets the context and next, and calling next() runs the rest of the chain
A database layer between the service and the store
A separate server that sits in front of the Task API

questions.q: A maintenance middleware returns a 503 response without calling next(). What is this called, and what happens to the route?
questions.explain: Not calling next() stops the chain there. Nothing after that middleware, including the route, runs.
options: Short-circuiting: the route never runs
Short-circuiting: the route runs, but its answer is thrown away
Bubbling: the route runs after the 503 is sent
A preflight: the browser asks again later

questions.q: In an HttpMiddlewarePipeline, how does priority decide the order?
questions.explain: pipeline.use(mw, { priority: -10 }) runs before a middleware with the default 0. Lower priority means an outer layer of the onion: it starts first and finishes last.
options: Higher numbers run first; the default is 100
Lower numbers run first and wrap the rest; the default is 0; equal priorities keep the order you added them in
The order is random unless every middleware has a priority
Priority only matters for middleware that short-circuits

questions.q: A middleware adds x-response-time to responses. It must also appear on 503 answers from a maintenance middleware. Where should it go?
questions.explain: A middleware only sees responses from the layers inside it. Put middleware that must see every response first, so even a short-circuited answer passes back through it.
options: After the maintenance middleware, with a higher priority
Before everything else (lowest priority), so it wraps the middleware that answers early
Inside the route
Anywhere: every middleware sees every response

questions.q: What does X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff protect against?
questions.explain: With nosniff, the browser must trust the Content-Type you send. Framing is X-Frame-Options, cookies over HTTPS is the Secure flag, and request floods are rate limiting.
options: Other sites showing your pages in a frame
The browser guessing the content type, so a JSON answer can never be run as a script
Cookies being sent over plain HTTP
Too many requests from one client

questions.q: Which headers from createSecurityMiddleware() stop clickjacking, where an invisible frame tricks the user into clicking your buttons?
questions.explain: Both say "no other site may show my pages inside a frame". Without a frame, there is nothing invisible to click.
options: Referrer-Policy and Strict-Transport-Security
X-Frame-Options: DENY and CSP's frame-ancestors 'none'
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Access-Control-Allow-Origin

questions.q: Your development server on localhost sends HSTS. When does that cause trouble?
questions.explain: Browsers only accept HSTS from an HTTPS answer. A plain-HTTP dev server can send it without harm. If your dev server answers over HTTPS (a local certificate or proxy), send max-age=0 there, so browsers forget it. In production, behind HTTPS, keep the long default.
options: Always: browsers then refuse http://localhost for a year
Only if the dev server ever answers over HTTPS: browsers ignore HSTS on plain http://, but after one HTTPS answer they refuse plain http://localhost for a year
Never: HSTS only works on port 443
Only in production, never on localhost

questions.q: Your CORS allow-list only contains your own web app. A script uses curl to call the API directly. What happens?
questions.explain: Even a browser request from another site got status 200 and the data; only the missing header made the browser hide it. CORS never replaces authentication or permissions.
options: The server refuses it with 403, because the origin is not allowed
It works: CORS protects users' browsers, not your server, and curl ignores CORS completely
The request never reaches the server
The rate limiter blocks it at once

questions.q: Why does createCorsMiddleware({ allowOrigin: "*", credentials: true }) throw a ConfigurationError?
questions.explain: credentials: true lets the browser send cookies along. With "every origin", any site could act as your logged-in users. List the exact origins instead.
options: Because "*" is not a valid string
Any website could then make requests with your users' cookies
Because credentials only work with GET
Because CORS needs at least two origins

questions.q: A teammate writes their own origin check: origin.startsWith("https://tasks.example.com"). What is wrong?
questions.explain: An attacker can register a domain that merely starts with yours. The allow-list in createCorsMiddleware compares whole origins exactly; never replace it with startsWith or a loose regular expression.
options: Nothing: it is the same as the allow-list
https://tasks.example.com.evil.example starts with that text and would be allowed
It is too slow for every request
It refuses your own web app

questions.q: Where should the CORS allow-list live?
questions.explain: The allowed origins differ per environment. Configuration holds them, and the code stays the same everywhere. The config lesson does exactly this.
options: Hard-coded in the middleware file forever
In configuration, so development can allow http://localhost:5173 and production only the real domain
In a cookie, so each browser can choose
In the request's Origin header

questions.q: Why must a public API have a rate limit?
questions.explain: A rate limiter counts requests per client in a time window and answers 429 Too Many Requests when the client goes over, usually with a Retry-After header.
options: To make every response faster
Without one, a single script can flood the API with junk or guess passwords all day
Because browsers refuse APIs without one
To replace authentication

questions.q: The limiter allows 3 requests per 60 seconds, and its window slides. What does that prevent?
questions.explain: Each check forgets only requests older than windowMs, so there is no fixed moment when the counter resets and a burst can slip through.
options: A client sending 3 requests in one second
A client sending 3 requests at 11:59:59 and 3 more at 12:00:00
Two different clients using the same allowance
The limiter using memory

questions.q: The Task API runs behind one load balancer, so every request seems to come from the balancer's IP. What is the safe fix?
questions.explain: Any client can send X-Forwarded-For and pick its own address. Only with trustProxy set to the real number of proxies does the adapter believe it.
options: Always read the client's IP from the X-Forwarded-For header
Tell the adapter how many proxies you run, for example createNodeHttpAdapter({ trustProxy: 1 })
Turn off rate limiting behind a proxy
Rate limit by the User-Agent header instead

questions.q: Why does the Task API use a gentle limit for every request plus a stricter one only for writes?
questions.explain: limitWrites only calls the strict middleware for methods that are not GET, HEAD or OPTIONS. A client that hit the write limit can still read its tasks.
options: Because GET requests cannot be rate limited
Creating tasks costs more than reading them, so writes get a lower allowance while reading keeps working
Because the stricter limit also handles CORS
So write requests skip the security headers

questions.q: The Task API runs as three copies of the same process, each with the in-memory limiter set to 100 per minute. What really happens?
questions.explain: The counts live in the memory of one process. With several copies you need a shared store; the security lesson covers that case.
options: All three share one count of 100
Each copy counts separately, so a client may get up to about 300 per minute
The limiter refuses to start with more than one copy
Only the first copy counts requests

questions.q: In the Task API pipeline, why does CORS come before the rate limits?
questions.explain: The CORS middleware answers OPTIONS preflights by itself. Placed first, those extra browser requests never reach the limiter. Security headers go before both, so every answer gets them.
options: CORS is faster than rate limiting
So a preflight is answered at once and does not use up the client's allowance
So rate-limited answers never get CORS headers
Because the rate limiter needs the Origin header

questions.q: When should you use @zudojs/middleware's createPipeline instead of HttpMiddlewarePipeline?
questions.explain: createPipeline works with any kind of context and reports whether the run succeeded, so one set of checks can serve a job, a CLI tool and, through a small adapter, a route. For plain HTTP middleware, stay with HttpMiddlewarePipeline, which knows about requests and responses.
options: For every HTTP route, because it is more general
For checks that must also run outside HTTP, such as in a background job that sends reminders
Only for CORS
Never: it is deprecated

questions.q: What does server.stop() do with a request that is already running?
questions.explain: That is a graceful shutdown: the door closes to new connections, and requests in progress get a full answer. The default wait is 30 seconds.
options: Cuts it off immediately with a 503
Lets it finish (up to gracefulShutdownTimeout), while refusing new connections at once
Restarts it after the server comes back
Waits forever until every client disconnects

questions.q: What is the right order in src/server.ts when SIGTERM arrives?
questions.explain: Requests in progress still use the store, so the server stops first. Then the modules stop, and the container is disposed last.
options: Dispose the container, stop the runtime, stop the HTTP server, exit
Exit with 0 at once; the OS cleans up
Stop the HTTP server, stop the runtime, dispose the container, exit with 0 (log and exit 1 on failure)
Stop the runtime, exit, then stop the HTTP server

questions.q: Your platform kills the process 30 seconds after SIGTERM. How should you set gracefulShutdownTimeout?
questions.explain: If the platform kills the process first, requests are cut off and the runtime never stops cleanly. Leave time for the runtime and the container after the server.
options: Higher than 30 seconds, to be safe
Below 30 seconds (for example 20 000 ms), so your shutdown finishes before the platform kills the process
0, so shutdown is instant
It does not matter; the platform waits for it

questions.q: This tiny runner works like a middleware pipeline. Finish trace(name) so the middleware it returns pushes `${name} in` into log before calling next(), and `${name} out` after it, and returns what next() returned. The program should print outer in, inner in, route, inner out, outer out.
questions.explain: Work before await next() happens on the way in, work after it on the way out. That is why the first middleware to start is the last to finish: the onion.
questions.expected: outer in, inner in, route, inner out, outer out

questions.q: Finish the maintenance middleware. When state.on is true, it must not call next() and return { status: 503 }. Otherwise it returns what next() returns. The program should print 200 503 routeCalls=1.
questions.explain: Returning without calling next() short-circuits the chain, so the route runs only for the first request.

questions.q: Finish cacheControl: call next(), then set headers["cache-control"] to "no-store" on the response it returned, and return that response. The program should print 200 no-store.
questions.explain: This is work after next(): the response only exists once the rest of the chain has built it.

questions.q: Finish runOrder: return the middleware names in the order a pipeline runs them. Lower priority runs first, a missing priority counts as 0, and equal priorities keep their original order. The program should print security, cors, rate-limit, router.
questions.explain: Sort by priority ?? 0. JavaScript's sort is stable, so cors and rate-limit (both 0) keep the order they were added in. Copy the array first so you do not change the caller's list.

questions.q: Finish allowOrigin: return the origin when it is exactly one of allowed, otherwise null. Do not use startsWith. The program should print https://tasks.example.com null null.
questions.explain: includes compares whole strings exactly, so a look-alike domain that merely starts with yours is refused. In a real app, createCorsMiddleware does this for you.

questions.q: Finish onlyWrites(middleware). It returns a new middleware (method, next) that calls next() directly for GET, HEAD and OPTIONS, and otherwise calls middleware(method, next). The program should print GET:ok POST:limited DELETE:limited OPTIONS:ok.
questions.explain: This is the Task API's limitWrites: reads skip the strict limit, writes go through it. A middleware that wraps another middleware is just a function that returns a function.
